name: Strawberries
description: Sweet, fragrant greenhouse berries from the northern farms, at their best in the cool months.
tip: Look for bright, glossy berries with fresh green caps. Don’t wash until just before eating.

name: Apples
description: Crisp orchard apples in dozens of heritage varieties, from sharp cookers to honey-sweet eaters.
tip: Ask growers which variety suits baking or eating. Store in a cool, dark place away from greens.

name: Peaches
description: Juicy stone fruit from regional orchards, soft and sweet when ripe.
tip: A ripe peach smells sweet at the stem and gives slightly when pressed. Ripen at room temperature.

name: Blueberries
description: Small, dusky berries from hillside bushes, great fresh or frozen for winter.
tip: Choose firm berries with a silvery bloom. Refrigerate unwashed for up to a week.

name: Lemons
description: Small, fragrant local lemons from farm groves, in season through the cool months.
tip: Heavy lemons are juicier. Unwaxed market lemons are perfect for zesting.

name: Figs
description: Soft, honeyed figs with a short season — catch them in late summer.
tip: Figs don’t ripen after picking, so buy soft ones and eat within two days.

name: Watermelon
description: Big, cooling melons from the lowland fields, sold whole or by the slice.
tip: Tap it — a deep, hollow sound and a creamy yellow ground spot mean it’s ripe.

name: Pears
description: Buttery orchard pears that ripen gently in the fruit bowl.
tip: Check the neck: when it yields to gentle pressure, the pear is ready.

name: Tomatoes
description: Local tomatoes from Qatar’s farms and greenhouses — the cool season from November to April is their peak.
tip: Never refrigerate ripe tomatoes — it dulls their flavour. Keep stem-side down on the counter.

name: Carrots
description: Sweet bunched carrots in orange, purple and yellow, pulled with their tops on.
tip: Twist off the leafy tops once home so the roots stay crisp longer.

name: Leafy greens
description: Hydroponic spinach, chard and salad leaves grown under glass year-round and cut the morning of market day.
tip: Wrap in a damp cloth in the fridge and use within three days.

name: Beetroot
description: Earthy roots in deep red, golden and candy-stripe, leaves and all.
tip: The leaves cook like chard. Roast the roots whole in foil until tender.

name: Pumpkins & squash
description: Local pumpkins and squash from the winter harvest — roast them or add them to a hearty harees.
tip: A hollow knock and a dry, hard stem mean it will keep for months.

name: Sweet corn
description: Sugary cobs best eaten on the day they’re picked.
tip: Look for green, snug husks and moist, pale silk. Cook the same day.

name: Aubergine
description: Glossy aubergines in purple, striped and white varieties.
tip: Choose shiny, heavy fruit with a green cap. Skin should spring back when pressed.

name: Peppers
description: Sweet peppers ripening from green to red, yellow and orange.
tip: Red peppers are simply fully ripened green ones — sweeter and richer in vitamin C.

name: Radishes
description: Peppery spring and autumn radishes, crisp and quick to grow.
tip: Remove leaves before storing. Slice thin with butter and salt on fresh bread.

name: Cucumbers
description: Crunchy field and glasshouse cucumbers, including small pickling types.
tip: Firm, dark green cucumbers without soft ends are the freshest.

name: Basil
description: Sweet Genovese and Thai basil, sold in bunches or as living pots.
tip: Keep bunches in a glass of water on the counter — never in the fridge.

name: Mint
description: Spearmint and peppermint for tea, salads and summer drinks.
tip: Plant it in a pot — mint spreads quickly in open beds.

name: Rosemary
description: A hardy, fragrant herb available all year round.
tip: Strip the needles by running fingers down the stem against the grain.

name: Thyme
description: Tiny-leaved, woody herb for roasts, stews and roasted vegetables.
tip: Dried thyme keeps its flavour well — hang a bunch upside down to dry.

name: Parsley
description: Flat-leaf and curly parsley, bright and grassy.
tip: Chop the stems too — they carry most of the flavour.

name: Chives
description: Mild, oniony herb with edible purple flowers in early summer.
tip: Snip with scissors straight over eggs or potatoes.

name: Farmhouse cheese
description: Aged and fresh cheeses from small local dairies, made on the farm.
tip: Wrap cheese in waxed or baking paper rather than cling film so it can breathe.

name: Bottled milk
description: Whole, non-homogenised milk in returnable glass bottles.
tip: Return the glass bottle next visit — most dairies give a deposit back.

name: Free-range eggs
description: Eggs from pasture-roaming hens, with rich orange yolks.
tip: Farm eggs keep well for weeks unwashed. Store pointy end down.

name: Farm yogurt
description: Thick, tangy yogurt cultured in small batches.
tip: Swirl in fresh berries and a spoon of local honey.

name: Raw honey
description: Unfiltered honey from hives in the orchards and wildflower meadows.
tip: Crystallised honey is still perfect — warm the jar gently in water to soften it.

name: Sourdough bread
description: Slow-fermented loaves from market bakers, baked before dawn.
tip: Store cut-side down on a board; revive a day-old loaf in a hot oven for five minutes.

name: Mushrooms
description: Oyster, shiitake and chestnut mushrooms from local growers.
tip: Keep in a paper bag in the fridge; brush clean rather than washing.

name: Sunflowers
description: Armfuls of cut sunflowers for the kitchen table.
tip: Cut the stems at an angle and change the water every two days.

name: Lavender
description: Fragrant bunches for drying, baking and sachets.
tip: Hang bunches upside down somewhere dry for two weeks.

name: Microgreens
description: Tiny seedling greens — pea shoots, radish and sunflower sprouts — grown year-round under glass.
tip: Snip just before serving. Keep the tray on a sunny windowsill and water lightly.

name: Khalas dates
description: Qatar’s favourite date: caramel-sweet Khalas, sold fresh on the branch in late summer and dried all year.
tip: Fresh rutab dates are soft and half-golden; keep them in the fridge and eat within a week.

name: Pomegranates
description: Jewel-red regional pomegranates that arrive as the heat breaks in autumn.
tip: Choose heavy fruit with taut skin; roll it on the counter before cutting to loosen the seeds.

name: Mangoes
description: Juicy regional mangoes, at their sweetest from late spring into summer.
tip: Ripe mangoes smell sweet at the stem and give slightly when pressed.

name: Grapes
description: Red and green table grapes from regional vineyards, a summer staple at fruit stalls.
tip: Look for plump grapes firmly attached to green stems; rinse only before eating.

name: Oranges
description: Winter citrus for juicing and snacking, brought in from regional groves when local lemons ripen.
tip: Heavier oranges hold more juice. They keep for a week at room temperature.

name: Guava
description: Fragrant pink-fleshed guava, lovely fresh or blended into juice.
tip: Ripe guava smells perfumed and yields a little; eat the skin too.

name: Mulberries
description: A short spring treat from farm trees — soft, dark and very sweet.
tip: They stain easily and keep only a day or two; buy them for eating the same day.

name: Sweet melon
description: Fragrant local melons from the spring harvest, before the summer heat.
tip: A ripe melon smells sweet at the blossom end and feels heavy for its size.

name: Okra
description: A heat-loving local crop that keeps farms productive through summer — perfect for bamia stew.
tip: Pick small, bright pods that snap cleanly; large pods turn woody.

name: Zucchini
description: Tender local courgettes, often sold with their flowers still attached in winter.
tip: Smaller zucchini have the best flavour; store unwashed in the fridge.

name: Cauliflower
description: Creamy-white winter heads from the northern farms, great roasted with spices.
tip: Choose heads with tight florets and fresh green leaves wrapped around them.

name: Cabbage
description: Crisp green winter cabbage for salads, stuffed-cabbage rolls and soups.
tip: A good cabbage feels heavy and squeaks when you squeeze it.

name: Potatoes
description: New-season local potatoes with thin skins, dug in late winter and spring.
tip: Keep them somewhere cool and dark, away from onions.

name: Onions
description: Brown and red onions from the spring harvest, sweeter than stored ones.
tip: Store in a dry, airy basket; they last for weeks.

name: Green beans
description: Slim, snappy beans from the cool-season farms.
tip: Fresh beans snap cleanly in half; cook them quickly to keep the colour.

name: Romaine lettuce
description: Crunchy romaine hearts from field and greenhouse — the base of a good fattoush.
tip: Wrap in a damp towel in the fridge to keep the leaves crisp.

name: Chilli peppers
description: Green and red chillies from local greenhouses, from mild to fiery.
tip: The smaller and redder, the hotter. They freeze well whole.

name: Sweet potatoes
description: Orange-fleshed sweet potatoes from the winter harvest, lovely roasted.
tip: Keep them at room temperature — the fridge spoils their texture.

name: Coriander
description: Fragrant fresh coriander, a must for salsas, soups and machboos.
tip: Stand the bunch in a glass of water in the fridge, loosely covered.

name: Dill
description: Feathery dill from the cool season, perfect with fish, rice and yoghurt.
tip: Use it quickly — dill wilts faster than most herbs.

name: Jarjeer (rocket)
description: Peppery local rocket, eaten fresh alongside grilled dishes.
tip: Young, small leaves are the mildest; larger leaves pack more pepper.

name: Purslane (baqla)
description: Juicy, lemony succulent leaves loved in fattoush and simple salads.
tip: Choose bunches with thick stems and glossy leaves; rinse well.

name: Labneh
description: Thick strained yoghurt from local dairies, drizzled with olive oil for breakfast.
tip: Keep chilled and use a clean spoon; it lasts about a week once opened.

name: Camel milk
description: Fresh camel milk from local farms — slightly salty, light and traditional.
tip: Buy it chilled and drink within a few days; it also makes a good laban.

name: Laban
description: Cool, tangy cultured milk — the classic drink for hot days.
tip: Shake well and serve very cold, with a pinch of dried mint.

name: Akkawi cheese
description: A mild white brined cheese made by local dairies, great with bread and watermelon.
tip: Soak slices in water for an hour to soften the saltiness.

name: Loomi (dried lime)
description: Sun-dried limes that give machboos and stews their deep, tangy flavour.
tip: Pierce the lime before adding it to the pot, or grind it into a powder.

name: Regag bread
description: Paper-thin Qatari bread baked on a hot dome, often with egg or cheese.
tip: Eat it warm from the griddle — it turns crisp within minutes.

name: Date syrup (dibs)
description: Rich syrup pressed from local dates, stirred into tea or drizzled on bread.
tip: Keep in the cupboard; it thickens when cool, so warm the jar in hot water.
